transcript:
Header: 2025-06-05 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Michael (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Daniel, Leah, Omar (Aurora)

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on prefix/prompt caching strategy — hit rates, cache key design, multi-tenant safety, KV cache behavior, batching interactions, quantization impacts, and private/VPC considerations. Agreed to run a 48-hour benchmark and share docs.

Topics: Prefix caching hit-rate targets, cache key canonicalization, tenant namespacing, eviction policies, cold-starts, warmup strategies, batching vs. latency tradeoffs, quantization-induced variance, security (KMS, audit logs), on-prem/VPC resource sizing.

00:00:03 Michael (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to do a deep dive on the prefix caching approach we discussed in the POC scoping. Priya will go through the runtime behavior and some tradeoffs.
00:00:18 Priya (SE): hi, thanks. i'll share my screen — i have slides but i'll mostly talk through how our KV cache / prefix caching works at runtime. apologies if the slide text is a bit dense.
00:00:29 Daniel (Aurora): no worries, we mostly want to understand hit rates and safety for our multi-tenant workloads. we have a couple tenant groups that share models but different prompt templates.
00:00:40 Priya: cool. high level: prefix caching stores the model's key-value state for tokens for common prefixes—basically we save the KV after the prefix and reuse it to avoid recomputing the prefix attention. this reduces per-token compute and latency.
00:00:55 Leah: what's a realistic hit rate we can expect? our templates are fairly stable but users append variable context.
00:01:05 Priya: in our experience, template-stable workloads can hit 70-95% for the cached prefix portion depending on granularity. typical target for production is 80%+ for templated prompts. free-text or highly personalized prompts drop that a lot.
00:01:20 Omar: what determines the cache key? we don't want collisions across tenants.
00:01:27 Priya: K yes — core idea: cache key is a canonicalized prefix fingerprint plus a tenant namespace. the fingerprint is SHA256 on normalized tokens after lowercasing/whitespace normalization and stripping ephemeral trace ids. tenant namespace prefixes the key, so multi-tenant safety is enforced at lookup time.
00:01:47 Daniel: and for shared model variants, do we shard by model version as well?
00:01:52 Priya: absolutely — key includes model_id:version:tenant:prefix_hash. that way a model rollout (v1->v2) doesn't cause invalid hits.
00:02:03 Michael: quick follow — normalization can be brittle if we change tokenization. how do you handle tokenizer drift?
00:02:10 Priya: we store tokenizer version and a small schema in metadata attached to the cache entry. when tokenization changes we invalidate or rehydrate. in Dedicated or Private deployments customers can pin tokenizer bin to avoid drift.
00:02:25 Leah: eviction policy? memory constraints are our worry.
00:02:30 Priya: LRU with weighted sizing — each entry is sized by KV bytes + metadata; hot prefixes are kept. TTLs also applied for ephemeral sessions. for very large tenants we support per-tenant quotas to avoid noisy neighbors taking all cache.
00:02:50 Omar: what's the cost/latency trade when batching and using cached prefixes?
00:02:56 Priya: we typically see prefix caching reduce per-token execution time by 20-60% depending on prefix length. For batching, there are two interactions: batching increases throughput but may add latency. we run micro-batching with adaptive timers so if a request hits cache (fast path) it's served immediately; if it needs KV loads there may be slight extra I/O. overall batching + cache usually gives net latency win and large cost win.
00:03:23 Daniel: any gotchas with quantization? we plan to run 4-bit quantized models.
00:03:30 Priya: good question — quantization can make cached KV slightly model-variant sensitive. we include quantization profile id in the cache key metadata. if you change quantization or rerun quantize with different seeds, entries won't match. also, in some quantization schemes the attention kernel behavior changes slightly and introduces tiny logit differences; we monitor quality and have regression alerts tied to eval prompts.
00:03:54 Michael: can we control cache TTLs per route?
00:03:58 Priya: yes — route-level config allows TTL, per-tenant quotas, and whether to enable prefix caching at all. For privacy-sensitive routes you can disable cache or encrypt entries with customer KMS.
00:04:12 Leah: encryption — if on our VPC/on-prem how is data at rest handled?
00:04:17 Priya: for Private deployments entries can be encrypted with your KMS/HSM; for Dedicated we offer KMS integration and at-rest AES-256 by default, plus audit logs for access. we also support field-level obfuscation before caching if you have PII in the prompt.
00:04:33 Omar: do you store full prompt or only normalized fingerprint in the cache?
00:04:37 Priya: only the fingerprint and optional small metadata — we avoid storing raw prompts by default. raw prompts used to rehydrate are logged only if configured and with consent.
00:04:48 Daniel: cold-start behavior — how do you warm the cache?
00:04:52 Priya: several strategies: proactive pre-warm with known templates, bulk rehydration during deploys, and on-demand lazy warm. for high-sla flows we recommend pre-warming key templates before launches. the benchmark we'll run can recommend a warm strategy.
00:05:10 Michael: any operational visibility? we want hit rates by tenant and route.
00:05:14 Priya: Console exposes per-route and per-tenant hit rates, latency breakdown (KV lookup time vs generation time), and token-level cost breakdowns. we also push metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.
00:05:25 Leah: multi-tenant safety again — how do you prevent cross-tenant leakage if a bug occurs?
00:05:30 Priya: we enforce namespace checks at the KV store layer, and we have access controls — cache reads require tenant-scoped creds. in Private deployments you can also run isolated cache nodes per-tenant or per-tenant-pool for strict isolation. plus we have test suites that fuzz namespace boundaries.
00:05:49 Omar: what about eviction races during high churn — could a tenant see anther tenant's data due to race?
00:05:56 Priya: not if namespace checks are atomic at lookup time. races can cause transient misses or extra recompute but not cross-tenant reads. we also recommend per-tenant quotas to reduce eviction storms.
00:06:10 Daniel: operationally, what's the memory footprint ratio for KV entries vs model?
00:06:16 Priya: depends on sequence length and model (KV size is roughly O(seq_len * hidden_size) per layer). ballpark for a 16k context model with a 512-token prefix, the cached KV could be several hundred MB per hot prefix; this is why we encourage prefix-length limits and shared prefix policies.
00:06:38 Michael: can we partial-shard entries across nodes?
00:06:42 Priya: yes, cache is sharded by key hash and we support replication factor and cold-store spillover. enterprise customers often choose higher replication for availability.
00:06:53 Leah: quality monitoring — you mentioned regressions on quantization. what's the alerting flow?
00:07:00 Priya: we tie evals to specific prompt sets. if model outputs shift beyond tolerance (ROUGE/embedding-distance thresholds) we trigger regression alerts to the platform and optionally rollback to previous model or quantization profile.
00:07:15 Omar: does prefix caching affect deterministic outputs for testing?
00:07:19 Priya: determinism is preserved since cached KV is just a saved state — but if you change any part of the pipeline (tokenizer, model params, quant) you will see diffs. that's why we include the exact artifact ids in the cache key.
00:07:31 Daniel: for our use-case we have mixed templates: some high-volume stable templates, others freeform. what's the recommended hybrid strategy?
00:07:40 Priya: enable prefix caching for the stable templates with longer TTLs and pre-warm; for freeform routes keep TTL low or disable caching, rely on batching/quant to cut cost. you can set route-level rules to auto-classify and opt-in based on hit-rate thresholds.
00:08:00 Michael: let's walk through a concrete example — banking chatbot templates vs account-specific notes.
00:08:06 Priya: banking chatbot greetings and regulatory preamble are perfect candidates. we store the preamble KV and only recompute per-user parts. for account notes with PII, we either disable cache or apply client-side obfuscation and encrypt with tenant KMS.
00:08:26 Leah: about the benchmark — what metrics should we collect?
00:08:30 Priya: recommended: per-route hit rate, end-to-end p95/p50 latency, tokens/sec throughput, cost per 1k tokens, error rate, and quality deltas on the eval set. we'll include a template.
00:08:45 Omar: can we scope the dev benchmark to our 3 highest-volume templates?
00:08:49 Priya: yes, that will show realistic wins. also please include cold-start paths.
00:08:55 Michael: security follow-ups — Daniel asked about KMS and audit retention. we'll get Security to follow up.
00:09:02 Daniel: thanks. couple more rapid-fire: do you store cache metrics in prod logs?
00:09:07 Priya: yes, we emit metrics and optional trace-level logs for cache hits/misses. logs can be forwarded to your SIEM in VPC/private deployments.
00:09:16 Omar: any limit on prefix length for caching in runtime?
00:09:20 Priya: we recommend a configurable prefix limit (default 1024 tokens) to protect memory. very long prefixes add little marginal benefit.
00:09:30 Leah: question on rollout safety — if we do a canary model change, will cache cause cross-canary contamination?
00:09:37 Priya: model-version in key prevents canary contamination. canary traffic uses the canary model_id:version and won't hit stable model's keys.
00:09:47 Michael: let's cover on-prem sizing briefly.
00:09:51 Priya: for Private/on-prem we recommend sizing cache nodes with 2-3x expected hot-set memory. we'll run a capacity plan after the benchmark. typical Dedicated config has separate cache-affine GPU pools to keep memory near compute.
00:10:08 Daniel: are there point solutions for very large static prefixes (e.g., entire regulatory docs)?
00:10:14 Priya: for very large static docs we maintain a persistent precomputed embedding/KV store and serve by document id; also we chunk large docs so you only load necessary chunks. that reduces memory spikes.
00:10:30 Omar: can we evict by LRU but also expire by least-recently-updated tenant policy?
00:10:36 Priya: yes — eviction policy is pluggable. you can use LRU, LFU, or custom tenant-priority policies.
00:10:44 Michael: ok let's fast forward to the later part of the call where we summarize and actions — quick recap?
00:10:50 Daniel: (laughs) it's been detailed, but helpful.
00:10:55 Priya: recap: prefix caching recommended for templated/high-volume routes, include model/tokenizer/quant ids in keys, namespace by tenant, apply per-tenant quotas, set configurable TTLs and pre-warm for launches. we'll run a 48-hour benchmark and share dashboards.
00:11:12 Michael: thanks everyone — we'll send the whitepaper and the benchmark plan.
00:11:18 Leah: thanks, talk soon.
